correctness.rationale: On Cr_n=K_{n,n} minus matching for n≥3, a zero on side A is permissible exactly when side B has at least two 2-labels, or one 2-label at a different matching index; if no 2-label on B, all A must be nonzero. Symmetric rule governs B. Disjoint exhaustive seven regimes indexed by sidewise numbers p,q of 2-labels give the exact displayed polynomial with H_n=(1+x+x²)^n−(1+x)^n−nx²(1+x)^{n−1} and Q_n=(x+x²)(1+x+x²)^{n−1}−(x+x²)(1+x)^{n−1}−(n−1)x³(1+x)^{n−2}. Same-index p=q=1 gives nx⁴(1+x)^{2n−2}, showing Roman minimum 4 with coefficient n; no other regime has weight 4 for n≥3. Independently enumerated all labelings for n=3,4,5 (3^(2n) possibilities) and reproduced all polynomial coefficients and minimum. Infinite n follows from exact case partition, not finite tests.

originality.rationale: Gangabylaiah et al. (2021) full primary paper supplies ordinary Roman polynomial for complete bipartite K_{m,n} but not matching-deleted crown graphs; deleting a perfect matching creates index-sensitive special vertices and changes all coefficients. Resultary earlier “Perfect Roman domination of crown graphs” already covers the min=4, n minimum functions corollary, and this part is NOT independently novel; it treats perfect Roman domination, not the entire ordinary Roman weight enumerator. Other Resultary complete multipartite / chain or restrained Roman results are different graph classes/conditions and do not imply the complete crown polynomial. Main graded polynomial survives best-of-knowledge originality with synonyms risk.
residual_risks: The minimum weight and its n minimizers are already available in the perfect Roman crown result and not claimed new.
An unindexed result under bipartite Kneser graph, matching-deleted bipartite graph or another synonym could contain the full Roman polynomial.
This is ordinary Roman domination, n≥3; no n=2 or other domination variants included.

value.rationale: Crown graphs are a canonical family, and a full ordinary Roman weight enumerator captures how one missing matching alters feasibility and the entire distribution, beyond a previously known Roman minimum. The seven-regime closed all-n expression is a useful exact benchmark for domination-polynomial methods.
